power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Nature connectedness (NC) refers to an individual's subjective sense of connection with nature and has a well-established link to overall health and well-being.
NC shows potential for being incorporated into future climate anxiety (CA) management interventions.
However, no study has reviewed the literature investigating the association between NC and CA.

Therefore, we conducted a systematic literature review to: 1) synthesise the empirical research and assess the evidence for associations between NC and CA using meta-analytic methods; and 2) identify factors that may influence this relationship, and the nature of their influence.
Following a systematic search of eight electronic databases from inception to April 2026, fifty studies met inclusion criteria.
Substantial heterogeneity was identified in NC and CA operationalisations.

We conducted random-effects meta-analyses using restricted maximum likelihood estimation (REML), using correlation coefficients (r) as the effect size metric and pooled across studies using inverse-variance weighting.
Meta-analysis indicated a significant positive moderate mean association between NC and CA.
NC and CA measurement instruments/items were selected as categorical moderators.
Subgroup analyses revealed 15 CA instruments significantly influenced the relationship between NC and CA.

Based on our findings we recommend: (a) the development and refinement of CA instruments and their conceptual alignment, (b) more diverse population contexts in this research area, and (c) the development of a clear theoretical framework for defining and conceptualising NC and its relationship with CA.
This review was registered on the PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (Registration ID = CRD420251063755).

text.text: This has since been replicated in a Canadian context, which also found NC to indirectly increase mental illhealth via CA (Thomson & Roach, 2023).

text.text: Taken together, this literature indicates that greater NC co-occurs with poorer mental health outcomes via increased CA.
However, other work suggests the relationship between NC and CA is more complex.

Academics have begun to conceptualise NC within a resilience framework, identifying it as a complex psychosocial determinant of mental health (Liu et al., 2016; Wells, 2021), due to NC's well-established link to better physical, mental, and social health outcomes.

text.text: NC and nature exposure is associated with fewer symptoms of poor mental health and decreased physiological arousal (e.g., Bakir-Demir et al., 2021; Bezold et al., 2018; Cai & Zhan, 2025).

text.text: Connection with nature is also linked to increased eudaimonic and overall well-being, happiness, life satisfaction, and quality of life (Capaldi et al., 2014; Pritchard et al., 2020; Wu & Jones, 2022).

text.text: Thus, although NC may increase CA, it is also beneficial for overall wellbeing.
Notably, other research highlights that the NC-well-being relationship is one with multiple mediators, and these likely also have implications for CA.

For example, NC facilitates social connections, which is in turn associated with increased psychological resilience, well-being, and prosocial behaviours (Henderson et al., 2024; Ly & Vella-Brodrick, 2024; Sitnik-Warchulska et al., 2025).

text.text: This complexity highlights the need for further research into the NC-CAwell-being relationship.
Before NC can be included in future CA management interventions, the nature of the relationship between NC and CA needs to be untangled.
While NC corresponds with higher levels of CA, it is also linked to several factors that may moderate the impact CA has on wellbeing through emotional, physiological, and social pathways.
Therefore, further investigation is warranted, and the first step is to identify the robustness of the simple association between NC and CA.

Despite the amount of research conducted involving NC and CA, as well as the significant variance in conceptualisation and measurement, no review examining their specific relationship with each other has been conducted.
Therefore, a systematic literature review and meta-analysis was conducted to examine the association between NC and CA.
We aim to systematically synthesise the empirical research and assess the evidence for, and direction of, associations between NC and CA using meta-analytic methods.

Previous research has indicated NC predicts CA (e.g., Cameron & Kagee, 2025; Grénman et al., 2025; Jalin et al., 2024; Whitmarsh et al., 2022), therefore we hypothesised NC will be positively associated with CA.

text.text: Due to the complexity of this relationship, we aim to identify factors that may influence this and the nature of the effect.

In addition to identifying any moderators in the literature, we also conducted moderator analyses to investigate how different operationalisations of NC and CA may influence this relationship across studies.

text.text: Information sources that were searched were Scopus, PubMed, APA PsycInfo, Web of Science Core Collection, Wiley Online Library, Cinahl, MedLine, and ProQuest.
Databases were searched individually, and search syntaxes were appropriately modified for databases.
Corresponding authors were contacted via email if additional information was required.

The initial search was completed in June 2025, and an updated search was conducted in April 2026, using the same databases, search strategy and eligibility criteria as the original search to identify studies published since the last search date.
Due to the constraints of the research team, only English language studies were included in the search.

Search dates were limited between 1990 and 2026; "ecopsychology" research was introduced in the 1990's (see Roszak et al., 1995), and has steadily grown, with most of the research about anxiety in relation to the climate taking place after 2007 (Pihkala, 2020).

text.text: Studies that incorporated a quantitative measure that is used to report on the relationship between NC and CA were included.
CA occurs across the lifespan and diverse populations and studies that investigated participants of any age, gender, or cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds were included.
Samples across multiple settings, therefore community and/or clinical samples, were included.

Any study design with quantitative measures of interest, including primary research peer-reviewed studies, longitudinal, crosssectional, case-control studies, cohort studies, randomized controlled trials, and quasiexperimental design studies were included.

Studies for which sufficient information could not be obtained to be included in meta-analytic methods, but still met inclusion criteria, were included in this review, but excluded from the quantitative synthesis.
Non-English language studies and those outside the time frame (1990-2026) were excluded.
Studies that did not report on the relationship between NC and CA using quantitative measures were also excluded.
Additionally, studies that were non-peer reviewed, non-randomized intervention studies, literature reviews, meta-analyses, editorials or case reports were excluded.
Our searches identified 3584 journal articles for uploading into Covidence.
A total of 776 duplicates were automatically removed by Covidence, with an additional 40 duplicates manually removed.
Title and abstract screening were conducted by the primary author (A.F.), full text review was conducted by two independent co-authors separately (A.F., L. O'B.).
The primary author resolved any discrepancies during the full text review after consultation with other research team members.
A total 50 articles met the inclusion criteria (see Figure 1).

Included articles demonstrated sufficient data compatibility, sharing similar outcome measurements, accessible correlational data (zero-order correlation coefficients; Pearson's r), and methodological quality.
It was therefore deemed appropriate to conduct a meta-analysis of random effects to provide a summary estimate of the relationship between NC and CA.
All meta-analytic calculations were conducted using R Statistical Software (v4.5.2; R Core Team 2025) and the package metafor (Viechtbauer, 2010).

text.text: Due to the way we define NC in this meta-analysis, studies that examined physical time spent outdoors (e.g., time spent in nature), were calculated together with NC measures (e.g., CNS) to create composite correlations.

A total of 16 new composite correlations were calculated; eleven new composites were created (across different measures), and five composites were calculated through collapsing subscales within measures (which we subsequently refer to as their overall scale name e.g., HEAS).

text.text: Sensitivity analyses were conducted assuming r = 0, 0.3, 0.5.
Each study reported a consistent low-to-moderate positive correlation across assumptions, indicating the conclusions are robust to plausible assumptions regarding the unknown inter-item correlations.
The results for the assumption r = 0.3 between items were used for each calculation.

A single study (Eichholtzer et al., 2024) investigated the effects of a nature relatedness intervention on various well-being outcomes in mixed method experimental design, however investigating intervention effects is outside the scope of this review.

text.text: Instead, each subscale outcome was retained and modelled as dependent effect sizes.
Therefore, a multilevel random-effects model was used to account for statistical dependence among estimates from the same sample.
Once statistical dependence was accounted for, a multilevel random-effects metaanalysis was conducted using restricted maximum likelihood estimation (REML).
Correlations coefficients (r) were utilised as the effect size metric and pooled across studies using inverse-variance weighting.
Effect sizes were interpreted according to Cohen's (1988) conventions, with correlations of approximately .10, .30, and .50 representing small, moderate, and large effects, respectively.

text.text: Statistical significance was calculated through twotailed tests with a significance level of .05.
Pooled estimates were reported using 95% confidence intervals.
Heterogeneity among studies was assessed and identified through Cochran's Q and I² statistic.
Publication bias was assessed through visual inspection of funnel plots, as statistical tests were not appropriate due to substantial heterogeneity detected.
Sensitivity analyses were conducted, using a leave-one-out analysis, to assess the individual studies influence on pooled effect size estimates.
Categorial moderator analyses were conducted to assess the influence of individual study characteristics on the overall pooled effect size estimate.
NC and CA measurement instruments/items were selected as categorical moderators, due to the significant variance in conceptualisation and operationalisation.
A joint moderator model was conducted first, before separate analyses were conducted.
Next, subgroup analyses were conducted to examine individual measurement instruments/items effects, using 95% confidence intervals and a significance alpha of .05.
We additionally tested the moderating effects of risk of bias, another categorical moderator, on the overall pooled effect size estimate of the relationship between NC and CA.
Correlations extracted from the included studies were transformed to Fisher's z prior to analysis to stabilize sampling variances.
All models were estimated using Fisher's z values.
Overall pooled effects and associated intervals were back-transformed Pearson's r for interpretation and presentation, whereas moderator coefficients were reported on the Fisher's z scale.

text.text: Informed by these results, a follow-up exploratory meta-regression including all studies was conducted using risk of bias as a moderator of the NC-CA relationship to examine whether the quality of the study contributed to heterogeneity or moderated effect sizes.
The omnibus test of moderation was not significant (QM(df = 2) = 0.99, p = .609), indicating effect sizes did not differ significantly across risk of bias levels.

Relative to studies rated as having low risk of bias, neither moderate-risk studies ( = -0.07, 95% [-.21, .08], p = .346) nor high-risk studies ( = -0.02, 95% [-0.22, 0.19], p = .875) demonstrated significantly different effect sizes.

These findings suggest that the influence of the outlying study is unlikely to be attributable to study quality alone and instead may reflect unique characteristics relating to that study or effect size.
Next, we examined whether risk of bias influenced the moderating effect of CA instruments on the NC-CA relationship.
The overall model was significant (QM(df = 27) = 53.62, p = .002).

However, neither moderate nor high risk of bias significantly differed from the low-risk reference category, and the contrast between moderate and high-risk studies was also not significant (moderate risk of bias vs low risk of bias:  = -0.10, p = .252; high risk of bias vs low risk of bias:  = -0.23, p = .085; high risk of bias vs moderate risk of bias:  = -0.13, p = .257).
Substantial heterogeneity remained (QE(df = 29) = 401.96, p < .001; I² =87.67).

text.text: Sensitivity analyses were conducted by the removal of the outlying effect size and high risk of bias study.

In contrast to the main-effect model, risk of bias as a moderator of CA instruments on the NC-CA relationship was significantly influenced by the exclusion of this study (QM(df = 26) = 31.62, p = .206).

The loss of significance following the removal of the influential high-risk study further suggests that risk of bias does not consistently explain the variation in the NC-CA relationship across studies and appeared to be largely driven by this single study.

Visual inspection of the funnel plot (see Supplementary materials) indicated effect sizes were generally symmetrically distributed around the estimated pooled effect size produced by the meta-analysis.
Studies with smaller sample sizes show greater variability in effect sizes, however there was no clear pattern of asymmetry to suggest substantial publication bias was present.

Although steps were taken to account for statistical dependence, these results should be interpreted with caution given the substantial heterogeneity detected and the inclusion of multiple effect sizes per study.
We contribute to the extant literature with a systematic review and meta-analysis to determine the nature of, and the variability within, the relationship between NC and CA.
Meta-analysis revealed a positive moderate significant association between NC and CA.
Results suggested CA instrument type could moderate the NC-CA relationship, whereas NC instrument type, and individual study risk of bias did not.
The positive association between NC and CA identified in our meta-analysis, indicates that individuals who feel more connected to nature also tend to report elevated anxiety about climate change.
This finding is conceptually consistent with previous research.

Forming a strong connection or bond with something often increases concern for its wellbeing; thus, greater connection to nature may lead to stronger feelings of worry and apprehension about climate change and its impacts (Kersten et al., 2022).

text.text: However, we wish to reaffirm that the positive association between NC and CA does not preclude the inclusion of NC in interventions designed to address CA.

text.text: This highlights the need for further investigation of other variables related to the NC-CA relationship, as discussed below in subsection 5.2.
Within our meta-analysis we examined whether NC and CA measurement-type, as well as risk of bias level, acted as moderators for the NC-CA relationship.
Risk of bias and NC instrument did not significantly influence the relationship between NC and CA.
Analyses using the whole sample indicated CA measurement type explained substantial heterogeneity in effect sizes, accounting for almost 40% of the between-study variance.
However, it should be noted that sensitivity analyses demonstrated this moderation effect was not robust to the removal of a high risk of bias study with an outlying effect size.
Therefore, while CA measures may contribute to the variability in the observed relationship between NC and CA, our findings should be interpreted with caution.
The focus of the CA instruments varied.

Most incorporated affective components, many covered behavioural, cognitive-emotional, and functional impairment, and some emphasised personal experience, and value orientations (e.g., biospheric concerns).
This review systematically prioritised identifying overall associations between NC and CA measures, using a standard quantitative approach of collapsing within and across scales.

Nonetheless, patterns in effect size and significance did emerge for different CA measures, suggesting a promising avenue for future research to qualitatively explore CA experiences in the context of NC.

Measures that included action-oriented cognitive items within a climate anxiety framing (e.g., "I am willing to control my consumption to realise the sustainable development") showed the strongest NC-CA associations, indicating these aspects may be more strongly related to aspects of NC.
In contrast, CA measures that were broader or diffused in approach, demonstrated weaker or non-significant associations (e.g., "I worry about climate change more than other people").

It is possible those instruments showing weaker or non-significant associations may be capturing aspects of CA that are less related to NC, as well as potential differences in measurement sensitivity, specificity and/or precision.
Our findings also suggest that conceptual alignment between NC and CA instruments can also influence the observed NC-CA relationship.

For example, in our analyses the strongest significant association between NC and CA was found in a study by Chen et al. (2023), which used the Environmental Awareness Scale (EAS; Despotovic et al., 2021) and the Connectedness to Nature Scale (CNS; Mayer & Frantz, 2004).

text.text: Additionally, the first item in the EAS is closely related to CA ("I am extremely worried about the world's environment") and sensitivity analyses were also conducted to assess its influence on results.

However, the other three out of the four items in the EAS strongly reflect action-oriented cognition and awareness (e.g., "I am willing to control my consumption to realise the sustainable development" and "The balance of nature is very delicate and easily upset") and were similar to the aspects captured within the CNS, which conceptualises an individual's relationship with nature as affective, experiential and emotional.
In contrast to the EAS, the HEAS had the weakest significant associations with three different measures of NC (CNS, NRS, and EID) across five studies.
These NC instruments focus on aspects of affective, experiential and emotional connections in the human-nature relationship.

Although the HEAS incorporates aspects of cognitive awareness and affective experiences including in relation to one's impact on the planet, it is primarily focused on affective arousal, persistent thought patterns, and behavioural impacts, rather than aspects of emotional and experiential connections to nature, and engagement within the climate change context.
This highlights the importance of considering the best operationalisation of concepts and alignment of measures when designing studies to answer specific research questions.
Relatedly, the CA instruments identified in our review had a negative cognitive, emotional and/or experiential orientation.

NC measurement instruments identified in this review are all positively oriented, aligning it with the way well-being is often measured, but not CA. Gago et al. (2024) found the orientation of the well-being instruments identified in their meta-analysis significantly moderated the relationship between CA and well-being, finding correlations to be stronger for negatively oriented instruments compared to those that were positively oriented.

text.text: It remains to be seen the extent to which CA may ameliorate the positive NC-wellbeing relationship, and how key factors like climate knowledge, social connection and PEB may add a moderating resilience to the stress of experiencing CA.
Recent literature suggests this will be a fruitful area of research.
For example, multiple studies show that both NC and CA are related to increased PEB and climate action (Ogunbode et al., 2022; Tam et al., 2023; Whitmarsh et al., 2022).

text.text: In terms of measure refinement, based on their apparent sensitivity for detecting significant associations in the current analysis, future research may benefit from specific validation work to identify a single-item measure of CA that has optimal utility in research examining relationships with NC and well-being.

Single-item measures are pragmatic and 57 cost-effective, and in our review, all single-item CA measures were significantly associated with NC, perhaps due to their ability to be easily adapted to distinct populations, good internal reliability, and licence for participants to effectively summarise their experiences (Allen et al., 2022; Zhang, 2020).

text.text: However, this is not to suggest that a single-item measure approach to CA should always be utilised in research.
As discussed, a nuanced understanding of the NC-CA relationship will require consideration of how the complex structures of NC and CA relate both to each other and to modifying factors.

A final limitation is that several studies in this review contributed multiple effect sizes in the meta-analyses. Hunter and Schmidt's (2015, p.442) formula for creating composite scores generally assume positive manifold when calculating composite scores.

text.text: Creating a composite score with negative inter-item correlations would potentially distort results.

While appropriate measures were taken to account for statistical dependence (utilising a multilevel random-effects model), the nesting of multiple results within studies may have increased the risk of biased estimates, and reduced generalisability and variance.
This review provides insights into the relationship between NC and CA, as well as the diverse ways in which these constructs are measured.
Overall, our findings indicate a positive association between NC and CA.
However, this relationship does not preclude the inclusion of NC in future health interventions, particularly where CA poses a risk for mental health.
Rather, our findings provide a foundation for future research to investigate variables that may mediate and/or moderate relationships between NC, CA and wellbeing.

While our findings suggest that NC is not a simple universal solution for problems with CA, NC may play a broader role in positively shaping people's well-being.

Future research should therefore build on our work to examine factors that may mediate or moderate the NC-CA-well-being relationship, as this work may have important implications for inclusion of NC in interventions targeting populations affected by CA.
Like the NC-CA relationship, the association between NC and well-being is only one component of a more complex system of relationships at play.
With a view to future research, a secondary aim of this review was to identify any factors that influence the relationship between NC and CA, and the direction of their 52 influence.

Factors influencing the relationship between NC and CA have not yet been a research focus in the extant literature; the available data used for this meta-analysis was largely salvaged from descriptive correlation tables or via email correspondence from authors.
Only one study included in our search investigated variables that may influence the NC-CA relationship.
Thomson and Roach (2023) tested climate knowledge as a moderator, 55 included in this review utilised a correlational research design, disallowing causal inferences to be made.
Additionally, nearly all of the included studies collected data through selfreported measures, which increases the risk of distortion effects such as response bias and method variance.
This emphasises the need for experimental and longitudinal research that incorporates objective measurement to further the understanding of the NC-CA-well-being relationship.
Secondly, most studies (75 -85%) investigating NC and CA were conducted in Western contexts, indicating population bias in the literature.

Climate change disproportionately affects developing nations, as they are more vulnerable to climate threats and possess fewer resources to combat climate change (IPCC, 2022; United States Global Leadership Coalition, 2021).

Future research should examine NC-CA-well-being relationships within more diverse populations to better understand the implications of concepts such as solastalgia and cultural variations in NC, thereby advancing understanding of NC and CA in relation to well-being.Thirdly, there were many inconsistencies in conceptualisation and measurement for both CA and NC.
Although the current study did not find NC to be a significant moderator of the NC-CA relationship, the conceptualisation and measurement of NC requires further development.

In this review, NC was categorised into 22 different operationalisations and while many of the studies included NC measures with similar qualities and characteristics, a universal definition of NC is still lacking (seeTiscareno-Osorno et al., 2023).

text.text: As previously discussed, CA conceptualisation and measurement also require further development.

Future research should continue to examine different CA instruments within the same sample population to clarify observed differences, determining if there is true conceptual variability between instruments or if measurement artefacts are present (seeHempel et al., 2025).
Given the complexity involved, both quantitative and qualitative research is needed to examine how different aspects of NC relate to different aspects of CA.

This research direction is situated within a broader research agenda needed to further the understanding of the NC-CA-wellbeing relationship, including the investigation of potential key moderators and mediators.
